reports.title: Do the TinyStories neurons survive new prompts?
reports.summary: 21 of 41 above-null neurons still beat 95% of fresh random directions on 12 unseen prompts with sampling.

blocks.text: The sweep found 41 of 8,192 neurons whose pushes beat every one of 256 random directions in their layer, on three story prompts. The obvious objection: three prompts and greedy decoding can be lucky. This study re-runs each of those neurons on prompts it has never seen, with sampling, against fresh random directions.
Setup

items: 12 new story openings, greedy decoding, plus 3 of them with nucleus sampling (top-p 0.9) under 5 seeds: 27 rollouts per neuron.
64 new random directions per layer, drawn from a different seed than the sweep's controls.
The same theme score as the sweep: the top five Poisson *z*-scores of words a push writes more often than the controls do.

reports.title: What happens when you remove a neuron?
reports.summary: 6 of 41 above-null neurons change the loss more than 95% of random neurons do when zeroed. Concept neurons steer strongly but are rarely necessary.

blocks.text: Steering asks what a neuron *can* write. Ablation asks what the model *needs* it for: hold the neuron at zero and measure how much worse the model predicts real stories [@meng2022; @heimersheim2024].
Single neurons

Each above-null neuron was zeroed over 300 held-out stories (up to 128 tokens each). 21 random neurons from the same layers give the baseline: 95% of them change the loss by less than 0.00144 nats per token. 6 of 41 above-null neurons exceed that.

head: Neuron
Theme
Δloss (nats/token)
KL
Tokens it helps predict
blocks.caption: Tokens it helps predict: tokens whose log-probability drops most when the neuron is zeroed (at least 5 occurrences; byte fragments that are not whole characters are left out).

blocks.text: Most concept neurons barely matter for ordinary prediction. A neuron can steer the story strongly and still be redundant, because other neurons carry the same information. This gap between *sufficient when pushed* and *necessary when removed* is the main caution for any single-neuron story.
Does the villain need its family?

The threat family is the 9 other above-null neurons whose themes include fear, danger or meanness: [L0·N80](#/atlas/L0/N80), [L0·N129](#/atlas/L0/N129), [L0·N454](#/atlas/L0/N454), [L0·N945](#/atlas/L0/N945), [L1·N878](#/atlas/L1/N878), [L2·N113](#/atlas/L2/N113), [L4·N803](#/atlas/L4/N803), [L6·N545](#/atlas/L6/N545), [L6·N967](#/atlas/L6/N967). The villain neuron [L6·N179](#/atlas/L6/N179) was pushed by one window on 12 held-out prompts, with and without the family zeroed.

The villain neuron's inputs and outputs

Upstream neurons were ranked by gradient × activation on [L6·N179](#/atlas/L6/N179) over the 40 stories where it fires most, and the top 25 were then ablated for real [@wang2022]. reports.title: 8 million, 800 million, 4 billion: what scale changes
reports.summary: TinyStories-8M, Qwen3.5-0.8B and the Qwen3.5-4B reference side by side: windows, finalists and what carries over.

blocks.text: The same question, does pushing one neuron write a recognisable theme, asked of three models two orders of magnitude apart.
What carries over

items: In every model a neuron's push is meaningful only next to random pushes of the same size. Random directions write themes too, often vivid ones.

The pushes that work are smaller than the residual stream itself: TinyStories windows are 0.4 to 0.8 residual norms, and the 4B alien neuron was recovered at 0.74. Beyond about one norm, every direction degrades the text.

Concept neurons are not confined to one depth. Above-null neurons per TinyStories layer: layer 0 12, layer 1 5, layer 2 4, layer 3 6, layer 4 2, layer 5 0, layer 6 8, layer 7 4. The 4B alien neuron sits in layer 22 of 32.

blocks.text: What changes

items: TinyStories writes only children's stories, so its themes are story beats (a villain, a loud noise, a moral). The Qwen models write chat answers, so a push changes what the assistant says about itself.
Residual norms grow steeply with depth in Qwen3.5-0.8B and jump in the last layer, where a few massive activations act like biases [@sun2024]. Pushes are sized per layer for this reason.

Superposition lets a model store more features than it has neurons [@elhage2022], so a clean single-neuron concept is a notable find at any scale. That is why the 4B alien neuron drew attention, and why each candidate here is checked against random pushes [@neuronexplorer].

reports.title: Literature review
reports.summary: 28 papers and tools, from key-value memories to refusal directions, and what this site takes from each.

blocks.text: The papers and tools behind the site, grouped by the question each one answers. Each entry says what the site takes from it.
What a neuron is
A feed-forward neuron reads a pattern from the residual stream and writes a direction back into it. That written direction can be read as a set of words.

items: **Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories** (Geva, Schuster, Berant & Levy, 2020) [@geva2021]. Reads each MLP neuron as a key (the input pattern it detects) and a value (a distribution over next tokens it writes). The atlas's contexts and logit lens show these two halves.

**Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Build Predictions by Promoting Concepts in the Vocabulary Space** (Geva, Caciularu, Wang & Goldberg, 2022) [@geva2022]. Shows that individual value vectors promote human-readable concepts in vocabulary space, and that adding them changes generations. This is the basis for pushing a neuron along its output direction.

**Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers** (Dai, Dong, Hao, Sui, Chang & Wei, 2021) [@dai2021]. Attributes facts to a few MLP neurons and edits them by suppressing or amplifying those neurons. An early example of single-neuron ablation and amplification.

**Neurons in Large Language Models: Dead, N-gram, Positional** (Voita, Ferrando & Nalmpantis, 2023) [@voita2023]. Finds many dead neurons and many token detectors in OPT models. A reminder that most neurons are not concept neurons, which matches the low above-null rate here.

**Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing** (Gurnee, Nanda, Pauly, Harvey, Troitskii & Bertsimas, 2023) [@gurnee2023]. Uses sparse probes to find neurons for specific features and shows that many features are spread over several neurons. Motivates the family ablations.

**Universal Neurons in GPT2 Language Models** (Gurnee, Horsley, Guo, Kheirkhah, Sun, Hathaway, Nanda & Bertsimas, 2024) [@gurnee2024]. Finds neurons that recur across GPT-2 models trained from different seeds, including families that suppress or promote token classes. Context for comparing neurons across models.

blocks.text: Why single neurons mislead
Networks pack more features than neurons, so most neurons respond to several unrelated things. This is why every claim here is tested against random directions.

items: **Toy Models of Superposition** (Elhage et al., 2022) [@elhage2022]. Shows that networks store more features than they have neurons by superposing them, which makes many neurons polysemantic. The main reason a striking single-neuron story must be compared with random directions.

**Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning** (Bricken et al., 2023) [@bricken2023]. Uses sparse autoencoders to recover more interpretable features than neurons in a one-layer model. The alternative unit of analysis this site does not use.

**Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet** (Templeton et al., 2024) [@templeton2024]. Scales dictionary learning to a production model and steers it by clamping features. Steering by features, not neurons, is the larger-scale version of this experiment.

**Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits** (Olah, Cammarata, Schubert, Goh, Petrov & Carter, 2020) [@olah2020]. Argues that features and the circuits between them can be studied like biology. The atlas borrows its specimen framing.

**Language models can explain neurons in language models** (Bills et al., 2023) [@bills2023]. Explains GPT-2 neurons automatically from their top activations and scores the explanations by simulation. Most explanations score poorly, another sign that top activations alone are a weak description.

blocks.text: Reading directions as words
The lenses on this site decode a neuron's output direction with the model's own unembedding.

items: **interpreting GPT: the logit lens** (nostalgebraist, 2020) [@nostalgebraist2020]. Decodes intermediate residual states with the unembedding matrix. The atlas applies the same idea to each neuron's output direction.

**Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens** (Belrose et al., 2023) [@belrose2023]. Shows the logit lens is biased in early layers and trains a per-layer correction. One reason the site also reports a steer lens measured by actually pushing.

blocks.text: Steering
Adding a vector to the residual stream changes what a model writes, with no training. A neuron's output direction is one such vector.

items: **Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering** (Turner et al., 2023) [@turner2023]. Adds a vector to the residual stream at inference time to change behaviour without training. The push used here is this technique with a neuron's output direction as the vector.

**Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition** (Panickssery et al., 2023) [@panickssery2023]. Builds steering vectors from the mean difference between contrasting prompts. The Qwen hunt's discovery stage uses the same contrast idea to find candidate neurons.

**Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency** (Zou et al., 2023) [@zou2023]. Reads and controls high-level concepts such as honesty through population-level directions. The top-down counterpart of single-neuron steering.

**Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction** (Arditi et al., 2024) [@arditi2024]. Finds that refusal in chat models is carried by one residual direction, and that projecting it out removes refusals. Heretic's Abliteration modifier implements this.

blocks.text: Causal tests
Ablation and patching test whether a component is needed, not just whether it correlates.

items: **Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT** (Meng, Bau, Andonian & Belinkov, 2022) [@meng2022]. Uses causal tracing to locate facts in mid-layer MLPs and edits them with a rank-one update. A model for testing claims by intervention rather than correlation.

**Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small** (Wang, Variengien, Conmy, Shlegeris & Steinhardt, 2022) [@wang2022]. Maps a full circuit with path patching and ablation. The villain-circuit study is a much smaller version of this method.

**How to use and interpret activation patching** (Heimersheim & Nanda, 2024) [@heimersheim2024]. Practical guidance on patching and ablation, including why zero-ablation can overstate effects. Applies directly to the ablation results here.

blocks.text: The models
The models studied, and the architectural quirks that shape how they are measured.

items: **TinyStories: How Small Can Language Models Be and Still Speak Coherent English?** (Eldan & Li, 2023) [@eldan2023]. Introduces the TinyStories dataset and the small models trained on it, including the 8M-parameter model the live atlas runs.
**Qwen3 Technical Report** (Qwen Team (Yang et al.), 2025) [@qwen2025]. Describes the Qwen3 family. Qwen3.5-0.8B, studied here, is a later member with a hybrid attention design.

**Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule** (Yang, Kautz & Hatamizadeh, 2024) [@yang2024]. The linear-attention layer that Qwen3.5 uses in three of every four layers. Its MLP neurons are still ordinary SwiGLU units.

**Massive Activations in Large Language Models** (Sun, Chen, Kolter & Liu, 2024) [@sun2024]. Documents a few huge activations that act like biases. Explains the very large residual norm in Qwen3.5-0.8B's last layer.

**Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks** (Xiao, Tian, Chen, Han & Lewis, 2023) [@xiao2023]. Shows the first token soaks up attention. The Qwen discovery stage skips the first token for this reason.

blocks.text: Tools
Software the pipeline depends on.

items: **Optuna: A Next-generation Hyperparameter Optimization Framework** (Akiba, Sano, Yanase, Ohta & Koyama, 2019) [@akiba2019]. The optimiser Heretic uses to search abliteration settings that cut refusals while keeping KL divergence low.
**Heretic: training-free language model modification** (Weidmann, 2025) [@heretic]. The open-source tool used for the refusal-removal study. Run here with its Abliteration modifier on CPU.

**neuron-explorer** (Lyra C (lyramakesmusic), 2026) [@neuronexplorer]. The project this site extends: neuron steering in Qwen3.5-4B, including the alien neuron L22·N2742 found by Bryson Tang. Its research log is quoted on the Qwen pages.
